applicability.equipment: The cranking test branches here cover the 2.3L, 5.0L and 5.2L engines.

guides.title: Compression testing: find a cylinder that cannot hold its share
guides.summary: Compare how well the cylinders build pressure, then use the result to choose the next test instead of guessing at an engine repair.
guides.introduction: Each cylinder has to squeeze its air charge before combustion can do useful work. A compression gauge checks that squeezing ability while the engine cranks. Think of it as comparing the cylinders on the same test bench: consistency matters, and the test only means something when the conditions stay the same.
guides.why: A weak cylinder can make the engine run unevenly even when its ignition and fuel systems are working. Compression testing helps separate a sealing problem from an electrical or fuel problem. A low reading identifies a direction to investigate; it does not by itself tell you to replace the engine.

when.summary: Use after a persistent running problem points toward a mechanical cylinder fault.
notes: This is a diagnostic test, not a scheduled tune-up item.
Use the engine-specific preparation in the linked engine-testing article. The 3.7L is not included in these cranking-test instructions.

prepare.title: Gauge and a repeatable test setup
prepare.detail: Use a suitable compression gauge and the equipment required by the engine-specific cranking procedure. The battery must be properly charged so later cylinders are not tested at a slower cranking speed.

prepare.title: Spark-plug access and clean working conditions
prepare.detail: Identify the correct plug procedure below. Dirt around an open plug hole can fall into the cylinder; organize removed plugs by cylinder so their condition remains useful evidence.

prepare.title: A technician-controlled cranking arrangement
prepare.detail: The test calls for a defined ignition-off auxiliary cranking setup. If you cannot establish that arrangement correctly, have a workshop carry out the pressure test; do not improvise a starter bypass.

steps.title: Confirm the engine and the complaint
steps.body: Record which engine is fitted and what happens when it runs poorly. Check the oil level and correct viscosity and confirm the battery is charged. These checks remove avoidable differences before you compare cylinders.

steps.title: Prepare the warm engine using its own test branch
steps.body: The test specifies normal engine operating temperature, ignition off, removal of all spark plugs and preparation of the intake and throttle. Follow the matching branch: the EcoBoost intake connection differs from the V8 arrangement.

steps.title: Measure the first cylinder
steps.body: Install the gauge in the first cylinder. Using the specified ignition-off cranking setup, allow at least five compression strokes and record the highest pressure. Also note how many strokes were needed to reach it.

steps.title: Repeat without changing the conditions
steps.body: Test the remaining cylinders with approximately the same number of compression strokes. Record the readings by cylinder rather than relying on memory. A slowing battery or a changed throttle opening can distort the comparison.

steps.title: Compare the low reading with the high one
steps.body: The cited engine test uses a lowest-cylinder reading of at least 75% of the highest as its comparison criterion. For example, a highest reading of 200 psi gives a 150 psi comparison point. This is a relationship between readings, not a universal target pressure.

steps.title: Investigate a repeatable low result
steps.body: Recheck the setup before blaming the engine. A follow-up cylinder leak-down test can help locate the escaping pressure. The engine-testing article also explains controlled follow-up checks; do not add oil or disassemble components without following that procedure.

steps.title: Restore the intake and ignition components
steps.body: Refit the plugs, intake parts and electrical connections using the matching procedures and tightening specifications. Confirm connector locks are engaged and that the engine runs normally after reassembly.

diagnostics.finding: One cylinder stays noticeably below the others
diagnostics.meaning: A local sealing problem is possible, but the test setup can also create a low reading.
diagnostics.next: Repeat the reading under the same conditions, then locate leakage before deciding on a repair.

diagnostics.finding: Two neighboring cylinders read low
diagnostics.meaning: Leakage between adjacent cylinders is one possibility.
diagnostics.next: Use the follow-up tests to distinguish a head-gasket path from valve or ring concerns.

diagnostics.finding: Every reading is low
diagnostics.meaning: A shared test-condition problem or broader mechanical issue may be involved.
diagnostics.next: Check battery speed, gauge connection and throttle preparation before interpreting the numbers.

watchFor.title: An unsafe engine should not be warmed for a test
watchFor.body: Do not run an engine with a serious oil-pressure problem, severe mechanical noise or overheating just to reach test temperature. Resolve whether running it is appropriate first.

verification.title: A usable cylinder record
verification.body: Keep engine identification, test conditions, stroke counts and pressures together. The record should explain why the next test is needed.

verification.title: Reassembly complete
verification.body: Verify every disturbed connection and plug is restored before returning the vehicle to use.

guides.title: Cylinder leak-down: listen for where compression escapes
guides.summary: Use controlled air pressure to distinguish leakage through the intake, exhaust, crankcase or cooling system.
guides.introduction: A compression test asks how much pressure a cylinder can build. A leak-down test asks where pressure escapes when the cylinder should be sealed. With the piston correctly positioned and the valves closed, a tester feeds controlled air into the cylinder and measures the loss.
guides.why: Different escape routes point toward different parts of the engine. Listening at the intake, exhaust and crankcase helps narrow the investigation before a large repair. The result is most useful alongside the earlier compression readings and the original symptoms.

when.summary: Use to investigate a repeatable low-compression result or suspected cylinder sealing fault.
notes: There is no routine mileage interval for this test.
Positioning the crankshaft and managing compressed air require workshop competence.

prepare.title: Cylinder leakage tester and regulated air
prepare.detail: Use a tester with the correct spark-plug-hole adapter and follow its setup instructions. The scale and air supply must be set correctly before comparing cylinders.

prepare.title: Correct cylinder position
prepare.detail: Identify top dead center on the compression stroke, when both valves should be closed. The piston reaches the top on another stroke too, so position alone is not enough.

prepare.title: Safe control of engine movement
prepare.detail: Compressed air can turn the engine if the piston is not held in the correct position. Keep hands and tools clear and establish a safe crankshaft-control arrangement before admitting air.

steps.title: Choose the cylinder from the evidence
steps.body: Start with the cylinder implicated by compression readings, plug condition or other mechanical checks. Label your measurements so you can compare that cylinder with the rest.

steps.title: Prepare spark-plug access
steps.body: Follow the correct engine-specific plug procedure. Fit the tester adapter without damaging the threads and keep debris out of the open cylinder.

steps.title: Set the piston at compression top dead center
steps.body: Confirm the cylinder is on its compression stroke. A valve held open by the wrong crank position can make a healthy cylinder appear to leak badly.

steps.title: Apply air in a controlled way
steps.body: Set up and connect the tester as its instructions require, while maintaining control of the crankshaft. Record the leakage reading once the test is stable. The linked engine test treats leakage above 20% as excessive; a result still needs a location and a cause.

steps.title: Listen at the possible escape routes
steps.body: Air heard at the intake suggests an intake-valve path; air at the tailpipe suggests an exhaust-valve path. Air at the crankcase ventilation connection points toward leakage past the pistons and rings. These observations guide further inspection rather than prove a particular part has failed.

steps.title: Check for a path into another cylinder or the cooling system
steps.body: Air at an adjacent open plug hole can indicate a path between cylinders. Bubbles in the cooling system can indicate a combustion-to-coolant path. Never open a hot or pressurized cooling system to make this observation.

steps.title: Release pressure before moving to the next cylinder
steps.body: Remove test pressure before changing connections or crank position. Refit the plugs and disturbed components with their matching procedure once testing is complete.

diagnostics.finding: Air is strongest at the intake
diagnostics.meaning: An intake valve may not be sealing, or the crank position may be wrong.
diagnostics.next: Reconfirm compression top dead center before investigating the valve.

diagnostics.finding: Air is strongest at the tailpipe
diagnostics.meaning: An exhaust-valve sealing path is possible.
diagnostics.next: Confirm the setup and compare with other cylinder evidence.

diagnostics.finding: Air reaches a neighboring plug hole or coolant
diagnostics.meaning: A head-gasket, head or block path is possible.
diagnostics.next: Document the route and carry out the relevant mechanical inspection before choosing parts.

watchFor.title: A percentage is only part of the result
watchFor.body: Test setup, crank position and the location of the air loss all matter. Avoid turning one gauge number into an unsupported engine-replacement decision.

verification.title: Record the route, not just the reading
verification.body: Keep the percentage, cylinder, piston position and where air was heard together. That makes the next inspection much more focused.

guides.title: EcoBoost oil pressure: measure the pressure behind the warning
guides.summary: Use a mechanical gauge to check actual hot oil pressure before deciding whether the switch, oil supply or engine needs attention.
guides.introduction: The oil pump sends oil through passages that feed the engine bearings and other moving parts. The warning switch reports a pressure condition; it is not a complete measurement of how the lubrication system behaves. A mechanical gauge lets you compare real pressure with the engine specification.
guides.why: Replacing the warning switch will not fix a genuine pressure loss. Measuring first helps distinguish an indication problem from low oil supply, pump trouble or excessive internal clearance. This guide is specific to the 2.3L test arrangement.

when.summary: Investigate an oil-pressure warning or a lubrication concern before continued driving.
notes: This is a diagnostic job, not a routine pressure check at every oil change.
Stop the engine when an oil-pressure warning or severe lubrication noise appears. Do not keep it running simply to see whether the warning clears.

prepare.title: Mechanical gauge and matching adapter
prepare.detail: Use a gauge and fitting suitable for the oil-gallery test connection. Keep the gauge, adapter and port scrupulously clean.

prepare.title: Safe access and replacement switch
prepare.detail: The linked switch procedure specifies discarding the removed switch. Have the correct replacement available and follow its installation requirements.

prepare.title: Hot-pressure specification
prepare.detail: The 2.3L specification is 29–60 psi (200–414 kPa) with the engine hot at 2,000 rpm. Cold or idle readings are not directly interchangeable with this test point.

steps.title: Check the basics with the engine stopped
steps.body: Confirm the oil level and look for leakage or contamination. An empty or seriously contaminated lubrication system needs attention before the engine is run for a gauge test.

steps.title: Access the switch safely
steps.body: Use the proper lifting procedure where underside access is needed. Disconnect the switch connector and follow the 2.3L removal procedure, protecting the connector and the oil-gallery opening.

steps.title: Connect the mechanical gauge
steps.body: Fit the correct clean adapter and gauge at the test port. Route the test equipment clear of exhaust heat and moving components. A leaking connection can affect both the reading and the engine oil level.

steps.title: Measure only when it is appropriate to run the engine
steps.body: A technician should decide whether the engine can safely be operated. The specified measurement is made at normal operating temperature and the stated engine speed; shut down if the test reveals a serious pressure loss or distress.

steps.title: Compare the actual test conditions and result
steps.body: Record temperature condition, engine speed and pressure together. Compare the hot 2,000 rpm measurement with 29–60 psi (200–414 kPa), rather than comparing an unrelated dashboard indication or cold reading.

steps.title: Follow the cause of a low result
steps.body: The diagnostic paths include insufficient oil, leakage, the pump, pickup restriction and excessive internal clearances. A failed reading warrants that investigation; it is not proof that the pump alone is faulty.

steps.title: Remove the gauge and restore the switch connection
steps.body: With the engine stopped, remove the test equipment and install the replacement switch using its specified sealing and tightening instructions. Restore the connector, confirm oil level and check the repaired connection for leakage when a safe verification run is possible.

diagnostics.finding: Gauge pressure is low at the specified test point
diagnostics.meaning: There may be a genuine lubrication-system fault.
diagnostics.next: Stop further running as needed and investigate oil supply, pickup, pump and internal leakage.

diagnostics.finding: Gauge pressure meets specification but the warning remains
diagnostics.meaning: The indication circuit or switch may need testing.
diagnostics.next: Use the appropriate electrical diagnosis; normal pressure does not identify which electrical component is wrong.

diagnostics.finding: Pressure reading changes with a leaking gauge connection
diagnostics.meaning: The test setup is unreliable and oil is being lost.
diagnostics.next: Stop, correct the connection and restore the proper oil level before repeating the test.

watchFor.title: Keep dirt out of the gallery
watchFor.body: Material introduced through the gauge connection can travel directly into lubricated engine parts.

watchFor.title: Avoid mixing engine specifications
watchFor.body: These pressure values and this access arrangement apply to the 2.3L engine. Other engines have separate test conditions and hardware.

verification.title: A documented pressure result
verification.body: Record the gauge reading with the required temperature and rpm. Keep the result with the diagnosis rather than recording only “oil pressure checked.”

verification.title: A sealed, restored connection
verification.body: Confirm the switch connector, oil level and leak check after the gauge is removed.

guides.title: Where is the oil going? Build an oil-consumption diagnosis
guides.summary: Separate an external leak from oil entering the cylinders, then measure usage consistently before choosing a repair.
guides.introduction: Oil can leave an engine in more than one way. It may leak onto the outside, travel through the crankcase ventilation system, or enter a cylinder through worn or damaged sealing surfaces. Topping up keeps the level safe, but a useful diagnosis starts by finding which route the oil takes.
guides.why: Uneven dipstick checks can look like oil consumption, and an external leak can be mistaken for oil burning. A repeatable record helps separate those situations. It also gives a workshop better evidence than a vague report that the car “needs oil sometimes.”

when.summary: Start when repeated top-ups, oil fouling or smoke suggest unusual oil use.
notes: There is no single oil-use threshold here for every engine, driving style and operating condition.
Formal consumption testing is a controlled diagnostic exercise, not a new maintenance interval.

prepare.title: A consistent record
prepare.detail: Record mileage, the amount and specification of oil added, how the car was driven and any smoke or leaks. Keep the measurement conditions consistent.

prepare.title: The correct level-check method
prepare.detail: Use level ground and allow oil to drain back before reading the dipstick. The diagnostic procedure calls for at least ten minutes after a hot engine is stopped.

prepare.title: Access to the ventilation and filter systems
prepare.detail: Identify the fitted PCV arrangement and air filter. The EcoBoost oil separator and the V6/V8 valve arrangements are different components.

steps.title: Make sure the readings are comparable
steps.body: Check that the dipstick is fully seated and repeat the reading under consistent conditions. Adding oil immediately after shutdown can lead to overfilling because some oil has not yet returned to the pan.

steps.title: Look for external leakage first
steps.body: Inspect the engine for the origin of fresh oil rather than replacing the lowest wet seal. Oil can travel down the engine or along surfaces before it drips. Resolve an external leak before trying to measure internal consumption.

steps.title: Check the crankcase breathing path
steps.body: Inspect the relevant PCV hoses, connections, filler cap and dipstick seating. A disconnected or restricted ventilation path can change where oil mist goes. Use the matching component procedure instead of assuming every engine has the same serviceable PCV valve.

steps.title: Inspect the air-filter condition
steps.body: Look for a damaged or poorly seated filter as well as dirt. The filter must keep abrasive debris out of the engine; replacement is about restoring that barrier, not simply hiding a dirty element.

steps.title: Measure usage with a controlled test
steps.body: The engine-testing article provides a workshop method for establishing a known fill and measuring oil use against distance. Keep the car at the correct operating oil level throughout. Record top-ups accurately and retain the driving-condition information.

steps.title: Use cylinder evidence when internal loss remains likely
steps.body: Oil-fouled plugs, compression testing and cylinder leak-down results can help guide the next investigation. Normal compression does not eliminate every valve-guide or valve-seal cause of oil use.

steps.title: Repeat the measurement after the repair
steps.body: Use comparable conditions to check whether the confirmed repair changed oil consumption. A successful part replacement should produce a result you can verify.

diagnostics.finding: The level differs mainly when checking immediately after shutdown
diagnostics.meaning: Drain-back time may be changing the reading.
diagnostics.next: Repeat the check with the same waiting period and level surface.

diagnostics.finding: Fresh oil is visible outside the engine
diagnostics.meaning: An external path may account for some or all of the loss.
diagnostics.next: Find the highest fresh source and repair the confirmed leak before an internal consumption test.

diagnostics.finding: Oil-fouled plugs remain after external and ventilation checks
diagnostics.meaning: Oil may be entering particular cylinders.
diagnostics.next: Use the plug locations with compression and leakage evidence to focus the inspection.

watchFor.title: Do not overfill to compensate
watchFor.body: Maintain the correct level. Extra oil is not a repair and can create its own problems.

watchFor.title: Driving conditions matter
watchFor.body: High load and engine speed can change oil use. Keep that context in the test record instead of comparing unlike driving periods.

verification.title: An actual rate, with context
verification.body: The final record should show distance, oil added, measurement conditions and whether visible leaks were present.

verification.title: A result after corrective work
verification.body: Repeat the same measurement approach so the before-and-after comparison is meaningful.

guides.title: Engine ticks, knocks and rattles: find the source before opening it
guides.summary: Use when and where a noise occurs to separate accessory, mounting and internal-engine concerns.
guides.introduction: Sound travels through an engine, its mounts and nearby panels. The part that seems loudest from the driver’s seat is not always the part making the noise. A useful investigation records when the sound appears and narrows its physical source before any major disassembly.
guides.why: A belt-driven accessory, a loose contact point and an internal bearing can all create noises that seem to come from the engine bay. Sorting the pattern first helps avoid expensive work on the wrong system. Oil level and condition come early because a lubrication problem changes whether further running is appropriate.

when.summary: Investigate a new, persistent or changing engine-area noise or vibration.
notes: A severe knock, oil-pressure warning or overheating is a reason to stop running the engine and assess it before reproducing the symptom.
Noise diagnosis does not establish a scheduled replacement interval for chains, bearings or accessories.

prepare.title: A description of the pattern
prepare.detail: Record hot or cold operation, idle or raised speed, load changes and whether the sound follows engine speed or road speed.

prepare.title: Safe listening equipment
prepare.detail: A workshop stethoscope or remote listening equipment can help locate a noise. Position sensors with the engine stopped where needed and keep all probes, clothing and hands away from belts and fans.

prepare.title: Oil and diagnostic information
prepare.detail: Check oil level and contamination and record related fault codes. A code is supporting information, not proof that the named part is the noise source.

steps.title: Describe the sound before changing anything
steps.body: Write down what triggers it and where it is heard. A cold-start rattle, a warm idle tick and a vibration under load are different clues and should not be combined into one vague complaint.

steps.title: Check whether more running is appropriate
steps.body: With the engine stopped, inspect the oil level, contamination and visible damage. Address a serious lubrication or mechanical concern before a listening test.

steps.title: Inspect mounts, clearances and obvious contact points
steps.body: Look for damaged mounts, loose fittings and components touching the body or nearby parts. Contact can transmit normal engine vibration as an abnormal noise inside the car.

steps.title: Reproduce the condition safely and localize it
steps.body: A technician can use suitable listening equipment to compare accessory locations with upper and lower engine areas. Change one operating condition at a time so you know what altered the sound.

steps.title: Follow the system that the evidence identifies
steps.body: An accessory-drive concern goes to the matching belt, pulley or tensioner diagnosis. A noise concentrated at the cylinder head calls for upper-engine investigation; a lower-engine concern needs lubrication and internal-mechanical evaluation.

steps.title: Measure before deciding on an internal repair
steps.body: Where the investigation points inside the engine, use the relevant oil-pressure, cylinder or valve-train tests. The sound alone does not specify which bearing, chain or valve-train component to replace.

steps.title: Recheck the same conditions after repair
steps.body: Return to the original operating condition and compare the result. Also confirm that anything disturbed during access is secured and clear of moving parts.

diagnostics.finding: Noise follows engine speed while the car is stationary
diagnostics.meaning: An engine, accessory or mounting source is more likely than a road-speed source.
diagnostics.next: Localize it with safe listening checks and the accessory/engine diagnostic paths.

diagnostics.finding: Vibration changes when the powertrain loads its mounts
diagnostics.meaning: Mount damage or contact with surrounding parts may be involved.
diagnostics.next: Inspect mounts and clearances before attributing everything to internal engine damage.

diagnostics.finding: Noise accompanies contaminated oil or an oil-pressure warning
diagnostics.meaning: A lubrication concern may make continued running damaging.
diagnostics.next: Stop and establish the lubrication condition before further reproduction tests.

watchFor.title: Do not use belt removal as a casual experiment
watchFor.body: Accessory layouts and operating limits differ. Follow a specific diagnostic procedure if it calls for isolation; do not run the engine with drive components removed on a guess.

verification.title: Reproduce the original condition
verification.body: A quiet engine under a different load or temperature does not yet confirm the original concern is fixed.

verification.title: Keep the diagnosis connected to evidence
verification.body: Record the location, operating pattern and measurements that justified the chosen repair.

guides.title: Inspect a used oil filter: read the debris without creating it
guides.summary: Open and examine a removed filter carefully to look for evidence of internal wear or damage.
guides.introduction: The oil filter catches material circulating with the engine oil. Examining a used element can reveal debris that was not obvious in the drained oil. The challenge is keeping the inspection clean: metal made by your cutting method can otherwise be mistaken for material from the engine.
guides.why: A substantial amount of bearing material can justify further internal inspection, while a few particles alone are not an automatic engine-failure verdict. Filter evidence becomes more useful when it is kept with the oil-pressure, noise and repair history.

when.summary: Use when engine damage is suspected or a repair investigation calls for debris inspection.
notes: Opening a filter destroys it; this is inspection of a removed used filter.
The illustrated opening method is for a metal spin-on housing. A cartridge element must be handled according to its own housing and service procedure.

prepare.title: Correct filter removal and a replacement
prepare.detail: Remove the filter using the correct engine-specific oil-service procedure. Restore the engine with a suitable new filter and the specified oil before any permitted operation.

prepare.title: Filter cutter and clean collection area
prepare.detail: Use the proper filter cutter rather than a cutting method that sheds metal into the element. Have a drain container and a clean surface for laying out the parts.

prepare.title: Hand and eye protection
prepare.detail: The opened housing can be sharp. The inspection procedure also uses a knife and vise for separating parts of the element assembly.

steps.title: Identify and remove the used filter
steps.body: Keep the filter associated with its engine and mileage. Drain the remaining oil into suitable collection equipment so the element can be handled and inspected.

steps.title: Open a spin-on housing with a filter cutter
steps.body: Cut the housing away from its base using the proper cutter. Keep externally produced debris away from the element. Do not apply this can-cutting step to a cartridge housing.

steps.title: Separate the element and support assembly
steps.body: Follow the illustrated sequence for removing the support tube and separating the element and end caps. Keep the pieces on the clean inspection surface.

steps.title: Inspect the support tube
steps.body: Look for retained debris before spreading out the element. Document the amount and appearance of material rather than identifying an engine part solely from color.

steps.title: Open the pleats for inspection
steps.body: Spread the filter material so debris hidden in the folds becomes visible. Compare the overall condition with the examples in the inspection article; a few particles and a large accumulation of bearing material are different findings.

steps.title: Decide whether internal inspection is justified
steps.body: Excessive metallic debris calls for investigation of the engine, including the bearings where directed. The filter alone does not establish every failed part or the full extent of damage.

steps.title: Preserve the evidence and restore the oil system
steps.body: Keep useful photographs or the inspected element with the diagnosis. Refit the correct new filter and oil as part of the appropriate service procedure; do not restart an engine whose damage assessment requires it to remain stopped.

diagnostics.finding: Only a few particles are present
diagnostics.meaning: The inspection examples allow that a small amount can occur without catastrophic failure.
diagnostics.next: Consider the symptoms and other test results before condemning the engine.

diagnostics.finding: A large amount of bearing-like metallic material is present
diagnostics.meaning: Serious internal damage may be involved.
diagnostics.next: Follow the specified internal inspection path and determine the extent and cause.

diagnostics.finding: Debris appeared while cutting the housing
diagnostics.meaning: The opening method may have contaminated the evidence.
diagnostics.next: Do not treat newly produced cutting debris as proof of engine wear.

watchFor.title: A clean-looking filter does not clear every fault
watchFor.body: Some problems require pressure measurements, cylinder testing or other inspections even when the filter contains little visible debris.

verification.title: Useful, uncontaminated evidence
verification.body: Record how the filter was opened and what was found in the support tube and pleats.

verification.title: A clear next action
verification.body: Decide from the combined evidence whether normal service, further testing or internal inspection is appropriate.

guides.title: Trace an engine oil leak before choosing the seal
guides.summary: Find where fresh oil starts so a wet oil pan or bellhousing does not send you to the wrong repair.
guides.introduction: Oil follows gravity and airflow. A leak high on the engine can leave a wet patch much lower down, and old spilled oil can confuse the picture. The useful question is where new oil first appears, rather than which nearby part is easiest to blame.
guides.why: Replacing an accessible gasket will not help if the actual leak starts elsewhere. Cleaning and tracing establish a repair target before parts come off. That matters especially around the rear of the engine, where confirming a seal can otherwise lead to major transmission-access work.

when.summary: Use when fresh engine oil is visible, drops appear, or an external loss is suspected.
notes: Check the oil level before operating the vehicle. A serious loss needs attention before further running.
Oil seepage and a leak producing fresh drops are different observations; document what is actually present.

prepare.title: Clean inspection access
prepare.detail: Arrange suitable access to the engine surfaces and protect electrical components while cleaning. Underside work requires proper support using the lifting procedure.

prepare.title: Oil-compatible tracing equipment when needed
prepare.detail: For a difficult leak, the linked procedure specifies oil-based fluorescent dye and a suitable UV inspection light. Dye type, mixture and oil-level control are part of that procedure; do not substitute an arbitrary additive.

steps.title: Confirm which fluid is leaking
steps.body: Check the appearance and location with the fluid levels and operating history. Identify engine oil rather than assuming every wet area is an oil leak.

steps.title: Remove old oil from the inspection area
steps.body: Clean the affected engine surfaces so new leakage can be distinguished from residue. The inspection areas include the block, heads, valve covers and oil pan; access depends on the fitted engine.

steps.title: Follow the first fresh trace
steps.body: Inspect from the upper areas downward. Include the filter and adapter, pressure switch or sensor, covers and sealing joints. On an EcoBoost, oil lines at the turbocharger are also possible paths.

steps.title: Use the specified dye method if the source remains unclear
steps.body: Follow the linked fluorescent-tracing procedure, including the correct preparation and inspection conditions. Account for the added fluid and leave the oil at its correct level; overfilling creates a new problem.

steps.title: Confirm the origin before selecting a repair
steps.body: A wet bellhousing area does not automatically prove the rear crankshaft seal is leaking. Use the access and inspection sequence to distinguish the seal from nearby joints or oil traveling from above.

steps.title: Repair the confirmed path and repeat the check
steps.body: Use the engine-specific sealing procedure. Clean the area again and repeat the operating condition that produced the leak so a dry result means something.

diagnostics.finding: Oil is wet low on the engine but fresh higher up
diagnostics.meaning: The lower area may only be collecting the leak.
diagnostics.next: Trace upward and identify where the clean surface first becomes wet.

diagnostics.finding: Only old residue remains after cleaning
diagnostics.meaning: The original observation may include an old spill or previous leak.
diagnostics.next: Recheck under the relevant operating conditions before choosing parts.

diagnostics.finding: A small leak takes time to appear
diagnostics.meaning: The source may not become visible during a brief check.
diagnostics.next: Use the specified tracing method and a suitable observation period without running with an unsafe oil level.

watchFor.title: Avoid replacing seals by location alone
watchFor.body: Oil can move across adjacent assemblies. A repair should follow a confirmed origin.

verification.title: Recheck a clean surface
verification.body: Document the original source and whether fresh oil returns after the repair and the relevant operating check.

guides.title: Intake vacuum: use the gauge pattern to choose the next check
guides.summary: Understand what a steady, low or fluctuating manifold-vacuum reading can reveal without treating it as a stand-alone diagnosis.
guides.introduction: At idle, the engine draws air through a mostly closed throttle and creates pressure below atmospheric pressure in the intake manifold. A vacuum gauge shows both the amount of that pressure difference and how steadily the engine maintains it. The needle pattern can provide a useful clue about air leaks or uneven mechanical operation.
guides.why: A low reading can have several causes, and a moving needle is not a parts-shopping list. The value of this check is choosing which follow-up test fits the pattern. Engine condition, operating speed and altitude all affect interpretation.

when.summary: Use as part of a structured investigation of rough running or a suspected intake leak.
notes: The illustrated patterns are diagnostic clues that require confirming tests.
A turbocharged engine can produce positive intake pressure under boost; the warm-idle vacuum check is a different operating condition.

prepare.title: Suitable vacuum/pressure gauge
prepare.detail: Use the appropriate intake-manifold connection and a gauge suited to the test. Confirm the test connection itself is sealed so it does not introduce a leak.

prepare.title: Controlled operating conditions
prepare.detail: The test is performed at normal operating temperature and the specified idle condition. Record altitude and any engine modifications that could change the expected behavior.

steps.title: Confirm the operating complaint
steps.body: Record whether the engine idles poorly, hesitates or has another symptom. Inspect for obvious loose or damaged intake connections before connecting the gauge.

steps.title: Set up the manifold measurement
steps.body: Use the appropriate intake-manifold test connection. Keep hoses and equipment clear of heat and moving parts, and verify that the temporary connection is airtight.

steps.title: Observe the warm-idle reading
steps.body: Record both the reading and whether the needle is steady. Compare it with the diagnostic conditions and altitude guidance in the linked article; do not compare an idle reading with a boosted driving condition.

steps.title: Describe any movement carefully
steps.body: An occasional drop, a regular pulse and a broad oscillation are different patterns. If the instrument has damping, adjust it only as needed to make the movement readable without hiding it.

steps.title: Choose a confirming test from the pattern
steps.body: A low steady reading can suggest an air leak or a timing-related issue. Repeated fluctuations can point toward uneven cylinder or valve behavior. Use the other symptoms and appropriate mechanical or intake checks to distinguish the causes.

steps.title: Correct the confirmed issue and repeat the measurement
steps.body: Restore the intake connection after testing and compare the result under the same conditions. Confirm the original running complaint as well as the gauge response.

diagnostics.finding: A low, steady idle reading
diagnostics.meaning: An intake leak is possible, but timing and engine characteristics can also affect the reading.
diagnostics.next: Inspect the intake path and use the matching diagnostic checks before choosing a repair.

diagnostics.finding: Regular repeated needle drops
diagnostics.meaning: Uneven valve or cylinder operation may be involved.
diagnostics.next: Use compression or leakage evidence and the actual symptom to narrow the concern.

diagnostics.finding: The reading changes after fixing the test connection
diagnostics.meaning: The temporary connection may have been introducing a leak.
diagnostics.next: Repeat the test with a sealed setup before interpreting the earlier result.

watchFor.title: Avoid applying one gauge number everywhere
watchFor.body: Altitude and operating conditions matter. The complete interpretation chart belongs with the test conditions.

watchFor.title: Keep diagnosis evidence-based
watchFor.body: A gauge pattern suggests a direction; it does not prove a failed valve, gasket or sensor.

verification.title: Record the before-and-after conditions
verification.body: Keep temperature, idle condition, altitude context, reading and needle pattern together.

verification.title: Restore the air path
verification.body: Remove test equipment and confirm every disturbed intake connection is secure.

guides.title: Valve-train inspection: check the movement behind a persistent tick
guides.summary: Inspect the upper-engine mechanism and measure camshaft lift when diagnosis points to a mechanical valve-train concern.
guides.introduction: The camshaft lobes turn rotation into the movement that opens the valves. Worn or damaged parts can change that movement as well as make noise. Once a diagnosis points toward the upper engine, a visual inspection and a carefully mounted dial indicator help distinguish an actual mechanical fault from a sound alone.
guides.why: Opening a valve cover creates access, but it does not identify a failed part. Measurement adds evidence. Keeping the indicator aligned and checking its return to zero prevents a loose fixture or poor setup from being mistaken for a worn camshaft.

when.summary: Use after engine diagnosis identifies a likely upper-engine mechanical concern.
notes: These analysis branches cover the 2.3L, 5.0L and 5.2L engines.
This is an inspection and measurement job; timing or component replacement requires the matching full procedure.

prepare.title: Engine-specific valve-cover and plug access
prepare.detail: Identify the correct cover and plug procedures. Maintain cleanliness around the exposed engine and protect open passages from debris.

prepare.title: Dial indicator and secure holding fixture
prepare.detail: The indicator must sit in the prescribed orientation on the cam lobe. A stable fixture is essential to comparing lift readings.

prepare.title: Controlled manual crankshaft rotation
prepare.detail: Use the specified manual rotation arrangement. The test requires clockwise rotation; turning backward can disturb timing. Do not use the starter with inspection equipment positioned inside the exposed valve train.

steps.title: Confirm the diagnostic reason for opening the engine
steps.body: Use the noise and mechanical-test evidence to identify the relevant engine area. Record the original symptom so it can be checked after the work.

steps.title: Remove the correct cover using its procedure
steps.body: Gain access to the valve train while keeping the engine clean. The V8 has separate bank procedures; the EcoBoost arrangement is different.

steps.title: Inspect the exposed mechanism
steps.body: Look for damaged, severely worn or incorrectly assembled parts. The 2.3L branch includes camshaft, tappet, spring and retainer checks; carry out deeper access only through the matching procedure.

steps.title: Prepare the dial-indicator measurement
steps.body: Remove the spark plugs as required. Position the indicator on the camshaft lobe in the specified plane and secure the holding fixture so it cannot move during rotation.

steps.title: Measure from the base circle to maximum lift
steps.body: Rotate the crankshaft clockwise to the base circle and zero the gauge. Continue clockwise to the high point and record the lift. Keep each reading associated with its lobe and position.

steps.title: Check that the indicator returns to zero
steps.body: Continue to the base circle. If the gauge does not return to zero, repeat the setup and measurement rather than accepting a questionable reading.

steps.title: Compare with the applicable service limit and restore the engine
steps.body: Use the correct engine specification to judge the measurements. Follow the appropriate repair procedure if a component is outside its limit, then refit the plugs and covers correctly.

diagnostics.finding: The indicator does not return to zero
diagnostics.meaning: The measurement setup may have moved or been inconsistent.
diagnostics.next: Repeat setup and measurement before comparing with a service limit.

diagnostics.finding: A repeatable lift measurement is below its applicable limit
diagnostics.meaning: Camshaft or associated operating-component wear needs evaluation.
diagnostics.next: Use the matching camshaft and valve-train repair instructions; do not select a limit from another engine.

diagnostics.finding: Damage or incorrect assembly is visible
diagnostics.meaning: A mechanical concern is present, but its cause and extent still matter.
diagnostics.next: Inspect the related components and follow the correct access and repair sequence.

watchFor.title: Keep rotation direction correct
watchFor.body: The specified clockwise direction protects the timing arrangement during this test.

watchFor.title: An open cover is not permission to loosen timing components
watchFor.body: Follow the engine-specific timing and camshaft procedures before removing those components.

verification.title: A repeatable measurement sheet
verification.body: Record each lobe reading and successful return-to-zero check.

verification.title: Correct reassembly and symptom check
verification.body: Verify disturbed components are restored, then check the original concern under safe operating conditions.

guides.title: Replace the audio DSP module on SYNC 2/SYNC 3 vehicles
guides.summary: Access the audio DSP module behind the left-side trim, replace it and transfer its saved configuration to the new module.
guides.introduction: The audio digital signal processing (DSP) module handles audio-signal processing within the SYNC 2/SYNC 3 entertainment system. Replacement requires access through the left-hand scuff and cowl trim. The module's vehicle configuration must also be transferred, so the work begins with a diagnostic scan tool before the original module is removed.
guides.why: Configuration capture preserves the information needed by the replacement module. The trim must come away in sequence to expose its mounting area. On the specified manual transmissions, the clutch pedal position (CPP) switch is an additional access component that must be removed and restored correctly.

when.summary: When diagnosis calls for DSP replacement, or the module must be removed for other repair access.
notes: Configuration transfer is required when installing a replacement module.

prepare.title: Arrange configuration transfer
prepare.detail: Have a scan tool capable of programmable module installation (PMI). Capture the original module's configuration before removal so it can be downloaded into the replacement.

prepare.title: Identify the access branch
prepare.detail: Have an interior trim remover, suitable hand tools and a torque wrench for the module fasteners. On the 3160 or MT82 manual transmission, identify the engine-specific clutch pedal position (CPP) switch procedure before removing it for access.

steps.title: Begin DSP programming preparation
steps.body: For replacement, begin DSP PMI with the diagnostic scan tool and follow its on-screen instructions. Complete the configuration-upload stage before disconnecting and removing the original module.

steps.title: Remove the left-side access trim
steps.body: Release the scuff-plate clips with an interior trim remover and remove the plate. Remove the hood-release-handle bolt cover, then the handle screw and handle. Release the clips and remove the left-hand cowl trim panel.

steps.title: Clear the manual-transmission obstruction and remove the module
steps.body: On the specified manual transmissions, remove the CPP switch using the applicable engine procedure. Then remove the DSP mounting bolts, disconnect its electrical connectors and remove the module.

steps.title: Refit the module using its numbered fasteners
steps.body: Reverse the removal sequence to connect and mount the DSP. In its mounting illustration, callout 1 identifies the upper-left bolt: tighten it to 106 lb.in (12 Nm). Callout 2 identifies the two lower bolts: tighten these to 62 lb.in (7 Nm). Restore the CPP switch through the applicable engine procedure, then refit the cowl panel, hood-release handle, cover and scuff plate.

steps.title: Complete replacement-module programming
steps.body: When installing a replacement DSP, complete programmable module installation (PMI) with the diagnostic scan tool. Follow the on-screen sequence to download the configuration captured before removal into the new module.

watchFor.title: Configuration not captured
watchFor.body: Removing the original module before the required upload leaves the planned configuration-transfer sequence incomplete.

watchFor.title: Different bolts, different tightening values
watchFor.body: Match each bolt to the numbered mounting illustration before tightening. The upper-left and lower attachments have separate specifications.

notes: The CPP-switch access step applies to the 3160 and MT82 manual transmissions. Use the linked switch article for the engine fitted to the car.

verification.title: Confirm physical restoration
verification.body: Check that module connectors and mounting fasteners are secured, access trim and the hood-release handle are restored, and the CPP switch has been reinstalled through its applicable procedure.

verification.title: Record programming completion
verification.body: When a new DSP is fitted, confirm and record successful completion of the scan-tool PMI sequence and configuration download.

guides.title: Strip and rebuild the 3.7L cylinder head subassembly
guides.summary: Disassemble and rebuild either 3.7L cylinder head while preserving valve-component positions and renewing the specified bank-specific parts.
guides.introduction: The 3.7L engine’s aluminum cylinder heads carry the valves beneath dual overhead camshafts. The valves control gas flow and seal the combustion chambers; their springs close them, while stem seals control oil passage along the stems. This bench overhaul sequence covers valves, springs, seals and head-mounted fittings. Arrange the separate cylinder-head removal, timing and refitting work before beginning.
guides.why: Reusable valve components must return to their original positions. The specified spring-compressor arrangement controls spring force during collet removal and installation, and the seal installer guides the stem seal into place. Left-hand and right-hand heads have different fittings, so their rebuilding sequences must remain distinct.

when.summary: When an already-accessible 3.7L cylinder head requires valve-component service or preparation of a replacement head.
notes: This guide begins with the cylinder head already removed. Follow the separate head-removal, timing and refitting procedures to reach and finish this bench work.

prepare.title: Organize components and tools
prepare.detail: Identify the head’s side and provide marked storage for every reusable valve component. Use the specified compressor tools and stem-seal installer; this work requires competent control of loaded valve springs.

prepare.title: Prepare the required replacement parts
prepare.detail: Provide new exhaust manifold nuts, studs and gasket. The right-hand head also requires a new cylinder head temperature (CHT) sensor. If replacing a cylinder head, replace the secondary timing chain tensioners as directed through the Variable Camshaft Timing (VCT) Unit procedure.

prepare.title: Use the specified lubricant
prepare.detail: For stem-seal installation, have clean SAE 5W-20 synthetic blend engine oil meeting WSS-M2C945-B1.

prepare.title: Workshop capability
prepare.detail: 3.7L cylinder-head bench work; valve-spring tools 303-300, 303-350, 303-1249 and 303-1418; stem-seal installer 303-470; torque tools and component identification storage.

steps.title: Strip the left-hand head fittings
steps.body: For the left-hand head, remove the ground strap and bolt, then the exhaust manifold heat shield and bolts. Remove the manifold and discard its nuts. Carry out the linked manifold cleaning and inspection, discard the studs and gasket, and remove the timing chain guide pin.

steps.title: Strip the right-hand head fittings
steps.body: For the right-hand head, remove the exhaust manifold and discard its nuts. Clean and inspect the manifold, then discard the studs and gasket. Remove the timing chain tensioner arm and timing chain guide pins. Remove and discard the CHT sensor.

steps.title: Remove plugs and organize the valve parts
steps.body: Remove the spark plugs using the [3.7L spark-plug procedure](#/document/G1675559). Mark reusable components before separating them so each can return to its original position.

steps.title: Disassemble each valve position
steps.body: Use the specified compressor arrangement shown in the cylinder-head procedure to remove the valve collet, spring retainer and spring. Remove the stem seal, then the valve. Repeat this sequence at each valve position, preserving the component identification.

steps.title: Install the valves and stem seals
steps.body: Install each valve in its assigned position. Lubricate the stem seal with the specified clean engine oil and install it with tool 303-470. The dedicated installer provides the required installation method.

steps.title: Reassemble the springs and plugs
steps.body: Use the spring-compressor tools to install each spring, retainer and collet. Repeat for every valve, retaining original positions for reused parts. Install the spark plugs through the linked ignition procedure.

steps.title: Rebuild the right-hand fittings
steps.body: Install the timing chain tensioner arm and guide pins, then a new CHT sensor. Install new exhaust manifold studs and a new gasket. Fit the manifold with new nuts and complete both tightening stages specified in the cylinder-head procedure.

steps.title: Rebuild the left-hand fittings
steps.body: Install the timing chain guide pin, new manifold studs and a new gasket. Install the manifold with new nuts and complete both tightening stages. Refit the heat shield and ground strap, tightening their bolts to the specified values.

watchFor.title: Head replacement changes the tensioner requirement
watchFor.body: Do not reuse the secondary timing chain tensioners when replacing a cylinder head; the procedure warns that engine damage may result.

watchFor.title: Parts that must not return
watchFor.body: Keep discarded manifold hardware, gaskets and the removed right-hand CHT sensor out of the reusable-parts groups.

notes: The illustrated compressor setup shows the specified tools working together; a generic compressor illustration is not an alternative setup.

verification.title: Check the bench assembly
verification.body: Confirm all reused components occupy their original positions, each valve position has its spring, retainer and collet installed, and the correct bank-specific fittings are restored.

verification.title: Record required renewals
verification.body: Record the renewed manifold parts, right-hand sensor where applicable, completion of staged manifold tightening and the secondary tensioner replacement requirement if the head was replaced.

guides.title: Replace the left-hand engine mount: engine-specific access and support
guides.summary: Replace the left-hand engine mount using the correct lifting equipment, clearance procedure and reassembly sequence for the installed engine.
guides.introduction: The left-hand (LH) engine mount supports the engine while helping isolate vibration and control movement. Replacing it requires temporarily transferring that load to an engine support bar. The four engines share this principle, but their access work, lifting arrangements and connections differ.
guides.why: Both engine-mount nuts must be released for the specified lifting operation. Correct support protects the engine and surrounding structure; careful reassembly restores the mount, electrical grounds and any vacuum or oil-cooler connections disturbed for access.

when.summary: When LH engine-mount replacement or removal is required for an established repair.
notes: Select the procedure by engine before dismantling; lifting heights and mount-nut torques are not interchangeable.

prepare.title: Provide safe vehicle and engine support
prepare.detail: Use a hoist at the specified lifting points, with the vehicle in NEUTRAL. Never work beneath a vehicle supported only by a jack. This job requires confidence handling a supported engine.

prepare.title: Match the lifting tools
prepare.detail: Use support bar 303-F072. The 2.3L, 5.0L and 5.2L use lifting bracket 303-050; the 3.7L uses engine lift eye 303-1245.

prepare.title: Plan variant-specific supplies
prepare.detail: Have torque equipment and the applicable battery/access procedures available. The 5.2L requires new strut-tower cross-brace nuts and an engine-oil level check after its cooler hoses are reconnected.

steps.title: Establish the correct access route
steps.body: Follow only the engine branch below. On the V8 engines, verify engine identification when selecting replacement parts. Position the hoist using the [lifting procedure](#/document/G1663631), checking adapter clearance around suspension and underbody components.

steps.title: Remove the 2.3L mount and bracket
steps.body: Follow the [2.3L procedure](#/document/G1945804): remove the appearance cover, fit lifting brackets to both sides of the cylinder head, disconnect battery ground and remove the radiator top shield. Remove both mount-bracket nuts, disconnect the LH vacuum tube and remove the mount bolts. Install the support bar and raise the engine 26 mm (1.0 in). Remove the underbody shield, detach the bracket-stud harness retainer and ground wire, then remove the bracket fasteners, bracket and mount.

steps.title: Use the 3.7L body-style access sequence
steps.body: The [3.7L procedure](#/document/G1681518) begins with cowl-grille removal. On convertibles, disconnect the negative cable, detach its retainer, disconnect the positive cable and remove the cowl extension. For both body styles, remove the air-cleaner outlet pipe and air cleaner, fit the lift eye, remove both mount nuts and radiator top shield, then support and raise the engine. Remove the mount bolts and mount; no lifting height is specified here.

steps.title: Prepare and lift either V8
steps.body: For [5.0L](#/document/G1685321) or [5.2L](#/document/G1800274), disconnect both battery cables and remove the brace and its harness retainer where fitted. Discard the 5.2L brace nuts. Remove the 5.0L appearance cover and radiator top shield; remove the intake components and both mount nuts on either engine. The 5.2L also requires both underbody shields and oil-cooler hose disconnection. Support-bar feet must rest on body structure, not fenders. Raise 50 mm (2 inch), then remove the mount bolts and mount.

steps.title: Install the mount before settling the engine
steps.body: Tighten mount bolts according to the selected procedure. On the 2.3L, first position the mount and bracket without their bolts; install the mount bolts, start the bracket bolt and stud bolt finger-tight, tighten the other bracket bolts, then tighten the bolt and stud bolt. Restore the ground wire, harness retainer and underbody shield before lowering.

steps.title: Restore the 2.3L connections
steps.body: Lower the engine and remove the support bar. Reconnect the vacuum tube, tighten both mount-bracket nuts, restore the radiator top shield and battery ground, remove both lifting brackets and install the appearance cover. The 2.3L mount-bracket nuts require 125 Nm; the other engines listed here use 63 Nm.

steps.title: Complete the 3.7L or V8 installation
steps.body: After lowering, the 3.7L receives its radiator shield, mount nuts, intake components and cowl parts; convertibles reconnect positive cable, retainer, then negative cable. On the 5.2L, reconnect cooler hoses and restore both shields before the mount nuts. Finish each V8's intake, brace and battery work. Refit 5.0L cover grommets to the intake manifold before the cover. Check and adjust 5.2L oil level using Castrol EDGE Supercar 5W-50, WSS-M2C931-C.

watchFor.title: Body-panel loading
watchFor.body: The V8 support-bar instructions expressly prohibit placing the feet on the fenders.

watchFor.title: A connection left behind
watchFor.body: Pay particular attention to the 2.3L bracket ground and vacuum tube, and the 5.2L cooler-hose connections.

notes: The 2.3L coolant tube is omitted from an illustration for clarity; that note does not instruct its removal.

verification.title: Confirm fastening and restoration
verification.body: Check off the selected engine's tightening sequence, removed access parts, electrical connections and lifting-tool removal.

verification.title: Record the variant-specific result
verification.body: Record the engine branch used and, for the 5.2L, completion of the oil-level inspection and any adjustment.

guides.title: Replace the clutch master cylinder — left-hand-drive MT82
guides.summary: Remove the pedal-and-bracket assembly, replace the clutch master cylinder, inspect its pedal retaining clip and bleed the hydraulic system.
guides.introduction: The clutch master cylinder converts clutch-pedal movement into hydraulic pressure for clutch operation. Its connection to the pedal transmits the driver’s force, while the cylinder moves fluid through the hydraulic circuit. Replacement requires removal of the brake pedal and bracket assembly before separating the master cylinder from the clutch pedal. Bleeding completes the repair by removing air from the hydraulic system.
guides.why: The retaining clip keeps the pedal connection secure and must be inspected rather than automatically reused. Air in the hydraulic circuit compresses under pedal force, interfering with the intended transfer of movement. Brake fluid also damages painted and plastic surfaces, so fluid handling and prompt cleanup are part of the job.

when.summary: When the left-hand-drive MT82 clutch master cylinder requires replacement or removal for service.
notes: A clutch-pedal or release complaint alone does not identify the master cylinder as the cause.

prepare.title: Prepare fluid handling
prepare.detail: Read the product label’s cautions and available safety data. Protect painted and plastic surfaces. If brake fluid contacts either surface, immediately wash it off with water.

prepare.title: Plan the complete access and bleeding work
prepare.detail: Have both the pedal-and-bracket removal procedure and clutch-system bleeding procedure available before starting. The cylinder replacement is only the middle phase of the repair.

steps.title: Remove the pedal and bracket assembly
steps.body: Follow [Brake Pedal and Bracket](#/document/G1692562) to remove the assembly. This is the required access step before removing the master cylinder; use that procedure for its associated connections and installation requirements.

steps.title: Detach the master cylinder and inspect its clip
steps.body: Following the [left-hand-drive master-cylinder procedure](#/document/G1687295), remove the mounting bolts, disconnect the cylinder from the clutch pedal and remove it. Inspect the retaining clip for damage and replace it if necessary.

steps.title: Install the cylinder and restore the pedal assembly
steps.body: Reverse the removal sequence, restoring the pedal connection with a serviceable retaining clip and tightening the master-cylinder bolts to 89 lb.in (10 Nm). Reinstall the brake pedal and bracket assembly through its complete procedure.

steps.title: Bleed the clutch hydraulic system
steps.body: Complete [Clutch System Bleeding](#/document/G1704358) after installation. Reconnecting the cylinder does not remove air from the circuit; the specified bleeding operation is a required final phase.

watchFor.title: Damaged pedal retaining clip
watchFor.body: Do not refit a damaged clip. Its condition determines whether replacement is necessary.

watchFor.title: Fluid on trim or paint
watchFor.body: Wash spills off immediately with water rather than leaving cleanup until reassembly is finished.

notes: This master-cylinder procedure is for left-hand-drive MT82 controls. The shared pedal-and-bracket reference also covers the 3160, which does not extend the master-cylinder procedure’s applicability.
Use the bleeding procedure for its fluid and equipment requirements; do not assume a bleeding method from the cylinder’s simple mounting arrangement.

diagnostics.finding: The pedal connection’s retaining clip is damaged.
diagnostics.meaning: The clip is unsuitable for reuse.
diagnostics.next: Replace it before completing the master-cylinder-to-pedal connection.

verification.title: Confirm mechanical restoration
verification.body: Confirm clip inspection or replacement, the secured pedal connection, correct cylinder-bolt tightening and completion of pedal-and-bracket installation.

verification.title: Record hydraulic completion
verification.body: Record completion of the clutch bleeding procedure separately from cylinder installation so the required hydraulic finishing step is not overlooked.

guides.title: Adjust coupe door glass for seal engagement and quarter-glass alignment
guides.summary: Measure and adjust coupe door-glass height, fore/aft position and inward/outward alignment, then initialize the power window.
guides.introduction: Coupe door glass must meet the roof weatherstrip and adjacent quarter glass in a controlled position. The window also drops slightly when the door opens and rises into the weatherstrip when it closes. This job corrects mechanical alignment while preserving that operating relationship.
guides.why: A glass position that looks acceptable may still have incorrect seal engagement or a tapered rear gap. Recorded measurements separate those errors. Equal inward/outward adjustment of the regulator rails avoids binding, and initialization completes the repair after the mechanical settings are established.

when.summary: When measured coupe door-glass alignment or weatherstrip engagement requires correction.
notes: If the door was removed or replaced, check and correct its alignment before adjusting the glass.
Use the coupe procedure; convertible window equipment is outside this adjustment scope.

prepare.title: Prepare to measure and retain access
prepare.detail: Have reference tape, suitable measuring equipment and a torque tool for the clamp and rail fasteners. Keep a record of measurements at each specified location.

prepare.title: Select the access procedure
prepare.detail: Use the speaker procedure appropriate to the door side and audio equipment. Position the driver door module (DDM) aside where fitted, and retain access to the window control switch.

steps.title: Expose the adjustment points
steps.body: After any necessary [door-alignment correction](#/document/G1693219), open the door and remove the speaker. Remove the DDM bolts and position the module aside as applicable. Remove access grommets, adhesive tapes and the lower watershield. Install the window switch as directed, establish the full-up position and close the door.

steps.title: Establish the engagement measurements
steps.body: Following the [adjustment procedure](#/document/G1697266), place reference tape at the A-pillar location 245 mm from the outer belt-moulding base, and near the roofline 230 mm forward from the glass's rear edge. Open the door and record each tape-to-glass-top distance. Close it and record each tape-to-seal-retainer-bottom distance. Subtract the closed-door reading from the corresponding open-door reading.

steps.title: Correct height and fore/aft position
steps.body: Required engagement is 4 mm ±2 mm at the A-pillar location and 8 mm ±2.5 mm at the rear roofline location. Open the door, loosen both glass clamps, adjust the glass and tighten the clamps to 9 Nm. Close the door and repeat the measurements and subtraction until both locations meet their limits.

steps.title: Measure the rear gap and its taper
steps.body: Measure the door-glass-to-quarter-glass gap at 75 mm from the belt-moulding base and at 75 mm from the door-glass top. Each gap must be 9.8 mm ±1.5 mm, and the top-to-bottom difference must be within ±1.0 mm. If either gap or the difference fails, repeat the clamp adjustment and recheck engagement as well.

steps.title: Adjust inward/outward engagement
steps.body: With the door closed, lower and raise the glass to inspect weatherstrip engagement at the specified locations. Open the door. Follow the sequence for loosening the fore/aft glass-run nuts and adjusting both regulator rails equally, then loosening the lower regulator nuts and making equal rail adjustments. Close the door and cycle the glass again; repeat until engagement is correct.

steps.title: Secure the rails without shifting them
steps.body: Open the door and lower the glass. Tighten the regulator-rail nuts to 11 Nm without moving the runs. Tighten the lower bolt and nuts on the fore/aft runs, then their upper nuts, to 11 Nm, again preserving the adjusted position. Raise the glass fully and close the door.

steps.title: Recheck every adjustment and initialize
steps.body: Repeat the open- and closed-door tape measurements after final tightening. Recheck the rear gaps and cycle the glass to confirm weatherstrip engagement; repeat the appropriate adjustment if necessary. Remove the tape and reinstall the removed components. Complete [Power Door Window Initialization](#/document/G1957566), using its separate instructions for an existing motor. Keep objects and body parts clear during initialization: the glass closes with high force and cannot detect an obstruction during that procedure.

watchFor.title: Unequal rail movement
watchFor.body: Moving the front and rear rails unequally can introduce binding.

watchFor.title: Position changing during tightening
watchFor.body: Hold the established run position while securing its fasteners; tightening must not undo the adjustment.

notes: Use the coupe adjustment dimensions. The initialization procedure distinguishes existing and new motors and requires the door to remain closed for the learning sequence.

diagnostics.finding: Seal engagement or the rear gap is outside its specified range.
diagnostics.meaning: Glass height, fore/aft position or rear-edge alignment needs correction.
diagnostics.next: Adjust through the glass clamps and repeat both sets of measurements.

diagnostics.finding: Weatherstrip engagement remains incorrect after dimensional adjustment.
diagnostics.meaning: The inward/outward setting still needs evaluation.
diagnostics.next: Use the equal-rail adjustment sequence, then recheck all dimensions.

verification.title: Record final geometry
verification.body: Record both engagement values, both rear-gap values and their difference, confirming each meets its stated limit.

verification.title: Confirm operation and completion
verification.body: Confirm weatherstrip engagement through a lowering/raising cycle, restoration of removed components and completion of window initialization.

guides.title: Replace the cylinder head temperature sensor by engine variant
guides.summary: Install a new cylinder head temperature sensor using the access route and tightening value for the fitted engine.
guides.introduction: The cylinder head temperature (CHT) sensor provides an electrical indication of cylinder-head temperature to the engine controls. Replacing it renews the sensing component and restores its electrical connection. The sensor operation is brief once reached, but access differs substantially: the 2.3L uses an appearance-cover access route, while the other listed engines require intake-manifold removal.
guides.why: Every listed procedure requires a new sensor once the old one is removed. Access instructions and tightening values must stay with their engine variant. In particular, the 3.7L sensor has a different tightening value from the other engines.

when.summary: When diagnosis calls for CHT sensor replacement, or a removed sensor must be renewed.
notes: A temperature-related complaint alone does not establish that the sensor needs replacement.

prepare.title: Select the correct access route
prepare.detail: Identify the engine first. The 2.3L route starts at the appearance cover; the other engines require the corresponding intake-manifold access procedure. For manifold work, plan the required fuel-pressure release, battery disconnection and replacement seals from that engine’s procedure.

prepare.title: Prepare the replacement and tightening tools
prepare.detail: Have a new CHT sensor, suitable hand tools and a torque wrench capable of the specified low tightening values. For manifold access, complete the prerequisites in the applicable manifold procedure.

steps.title: Expose the sensor on the 2.3L
steps.body: Follow the [2.3L procedure](#/document/G1692141). Remove the appearance-cover nuts and cover. Slide the sensor insulator upward to reach and disconnect the electrical connector.

steps.title: Use the lower-manifold route on the 3.7L
steps.body: Follow the [3.7L sensor procedure](#/document/G1692249) and remove the [lower intake manifold](#/document/G1681524) using its complete procedure. Disconnect the sensor electrical connector once access is available.

steps.title: Establish the correct V8 access
steps.body: For the 5.0L, follow its [sensor procedure](#/document/G1692277) and [intake-manifold procedure](#/document/G1685326). For the 5.2L, use its [sensor procedure](#/document/G1802183) with the matching [5.2L intake-manifold access and refitting procedure](#/document/G1800279). The sensor article’s access link names the 5.0L; this separate 5.2L route keeps the fuel connections, new gaskets and staged tightening with the correct engine.

steps.title: Remove and replace the sensor
steps.body: With its connector disconnected, remove and discard the old sensor. Install the new sensor at 10 Nm on the 3.7L, or 11 Nm on the 2.3L, 5.0L and 5.2L. Do not reuse a removed sensor.

steps.title: Restore the connector and access components
steps.body: Reverse the applicable removal sequence. On the 2.3L, reconnect the sensor, return the insulator to its installed position and refit the appearance cover, tightening its nuts to 9 Nm. On manifold-access engines, finish the complete manifold installation procedure.

watchFor.title: Using the wrong torque
watchFor.body: Keep the 3.7L value separate from the other variants; a common component name does not make the tightening instructions interchangeable.

watchFor.title: Incomplete intake reassembly
watchFor.body: Sensor installation is only part of the job when an intake manifold has been removed. Complete that assembly's connections and installation requirements before returning the vehicle to service.

notes: On the 5.2L, use the linked 5.2L manifold instructions despite the 5.0L access title in its sensor article. A shared sensor torque does not make the manifold procedures interchangeable.

verification.title: Confirm the installation
verification.body: Confirm a new sensor is installed at the engine-specific torque, its connector is restored, and the applicable cover or manifold installation is complete.

guides.title: Confirm a heater-core leak and plan climate-control housing replacement
guides.summary: Leak-test a suspected heater core before removal, then replace it through the appropriate climate-control housing procedure.
guides.introduction: The heater core transfers heat from engine coolant to the cabin air. For this repair, it is serviced as part of the climate-control housing rather than as a separately available core. Replacing it therefore means removing the housing, transferring required components and installing the replacement assembly.
guides.why: Testing first establishes whether a suspected leak justifies housing removal. A heating complaint alone does not establish a leaking core: the climate controls also determine temperature, air distribution and blower operation. Correctly identifying the repair avoids committing to housing replacement on that complaint alone.

when.summary: When testing confirms a suspected heater-core leak or another established repair requires its replacement.
notes: A suspected leak must be tested before the heater core is removed from the vehicle.

prepare.title: Plan an isolated leak test
prepare.detail: Use the heater-core pressure-test equipment and adapters specified in the linked test. The core is filled with water for this check. Arrange coolant draining and refilling, and examine the hose connections before deciding the core itself leaks.

prepare.title: Arrange the housing repair capability
prepare.detail: Housing removal involves refrigerant recovery and instrument-panel removal as well as coolant connections. Arrange the required refrigerant equipment, replacement housing, specified new seals and correct oil accounting before dismantling.

steps.title: Rule out a hose connection leak
steps.body: Start with the [heater-core leak check](#/document/G1912328). Coolant from a hose connection can track along the tube and look like a core leak. Inspect both attachments and the original spring-type clamps; an unsuitable or overtightened replacement clamp can cause leakage or damage.

steps.title: Test the core before removing the housing
steps.body: Follow the complete isolated test: drain coolant, disconnect the vehicle’s heater hoses and fit the specified short test hoses. Fill the core and test hoses with water, secure the plug and adapter, connect the pressure-test pump and close its bleed valve. Apply 138 kPa (20 psi) and observe for at least 3 minutes. If pressure falls, check the test-hose connections first. Replace the core only when the pressure loss remains and those hoses are not leaking.

steps.title: Choose the matching housing route
steps.body: The [heater-core repair](#/document/G1676815) services the core as part of the complete climate-control housing. Select the housing instructions for [2.3L](#/document/G1701609), [3.7L](#/document/G1701617), [5.0L](#/document/G1701624) or [5.2L](#/document/G1800364).

steps.title: Remove the assembly with its systems protected
steps.body: Complete the selected housing procedure, including refrigerant recovery and instrument-panel access before disconnecting the housing. Protect open refrigerant ports against contamination. Disconnect the heater hoses and the specified fasteners, then remove the housing without treating any attached wiring, pipe or hose as a handle.

steps.title: Transfer and reinstall the required components
steps.body: Transfer components from the old housing to the replacement as required for the fitted climate controls. Follow the same engine-specific housing procedure for installation. Install new O-ring seals with the specified lubricant and account for the correct refrigerant oil amount; preserve the tightening values and finishing operations of that exact branch.

steps.title: Restore the serviced systems
steps.body: Complete the specified cooling-system fill and bleed procedure for the fitted engine. Finish the refrigerant-system work using its proper servicing procedures, then confirm the required housing connections and component transfers are complete. The leak-test result establishes why the housing was replaced; completion of the coolant and refrigerant work is a separate part of finishing the repair.

watchFor.title: Assuming weak heat proves a leak
watchFor.body: Cabin temperature depends on coolant heat and the climate-control airflow settings. Weak heat alone does not establish a leaking heater core.

watchFor.title: Contaminating open refrigerant connections
watchFor.body: Cap or otherwise protect open ports during removal, and remove those protections before reconnecting the system.

notes: Electronic Manual Temperature Control and Dual Automatic Temperature Control differ in operation; preserve the appropriate equipment during component transfer.

diagnostics.finding: Coolant appears at the heater-core tubes.
diagnostics.meaning: A leaking hose connection can mimic a leaking core.
diagnostics.next: Inspect the hose attachments and clamp integrity before isolating the core for testing.

diagnostics.finding: The isolated pressure test loses pressure.
diagnostics.meaning: Either the core or a test-hose connection is leaking.
diagnostics.next: Check the test-hose connections first. If they do not leak, replace the core through the housing repair.

verification.title: Record the reason for replacement
verification.body: Retain the leak-test result, when applicable, and the identified engine-specific housing procedure.

verification.title: Confirm installation completion
verification.body: Check required component transfers and completion of the selected housing procedure's installation and finishing operations.
